vsm1.1:43.1: 43. Here is an explanatory exposition together with a word commentary starting from the beginning.
vsm1.1:43.3:
A bhikkhu: a clansman who has gone forth out of faith and is so styled because he sees fear in the round of rebirths
(saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanatā) or because he wears cloth garments that are torn and pieced together, and so on.
vsm1.1:43.4: Restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint: here “Pātimokkha” (Rule of the Community) is the virtue of the training precepts;
vsm1.1:43.5:
for it frees (mokkheti) him who protects (pāti) it, guards it, it sets him free
(mocayati) from the pains of the states of loss, etc.,
vsm1.1:43.6: that is why it is called Pātimokkha.
vsm1.1:43.7: “Restraint” is restraining; this is a term for bodily and verbal non-transgression.
vsm1.1:43.8: The Pātimokkha itself as restraint is “Pātimokkha restraint.”
vsm1.1:43.9: “Restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint” is restrained by means of the restraint consisting in that Pātimokkha;
vsm1.1:43.10: he has it, possesses it, is the meaning.
vsm1.1:43.11: Dwells: bears himself in one of the postures.
vsm1.1:44.1:
44. The meaning of possessed of the proper conduct and resort, etc., should
be understood in the way in which it is given in the text.
vsm1.1:44.3: “Possessed of the proper conduct and resort: there is proper conduct and improper conduct.
vsm1.1:44.4: Herein, what is improper conduct? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, bodily and verbal transgression—
vsm1.1:44.6: Also all unvirtuousness is improper conduct.
vsm1.1:44.7:
Here someone makes a livelihood by gifts of bamboos, or by gifts of leaves, or by gifts of flowers,
fruits, bathing powder, and tooth sticks, or by flattery,
vsm1.1:44.8: or by bean-soupery, or by fondling, or by going on errands on foot,
vsm1.1:44.9: or by one or other of the sorts of wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddhas—this is called improper conduct.
vsm1.1:44.10: Herein, what is proper conduct? Bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, bodily and verbal non-transgression—
vsm1.1:44.12: Also all restraint through virtue is proper conduct.
vsm1.1:44.13:
Here someone “does not make a livelihood by gifts of bamboos, or by gifts of leaves, or by gifts of flowers,
fruits, bathing powder, and tooth sticks, or by flattery,
vsm1.1:44.14: or by bean-soupery, or by fondling, or by going on errands on foot,
vsm1.1:44.15: or by one or other of the sorts of wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddhas—this is called proper conduct.”
vsm1.1:45.1: 45. “Proper resort: there is proper resort and improper resort.
vsm1.1:45.2:
Herein, what is improper resort? Here someone has prostitutes as resort, or he has widows,
old maids, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, or taverns as resort;
vsm1.1:45.3: or he dwells associated with kings, kings' ministers, sectarians, sectarians' disciples, in unbecoming association with laymen;
vsm1.1:45.4:
or he cultivates, frequents, honours, such families as are faithless, untrusting, abusive and rude, who wish harm, wish ill,
wish woe, wish no surcease of bondage, for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, for male and female devotees—this is called improper resort.
vsm1.1:45.5: Herein, what is proper resort? Here someone does not have prostitutes as resort … or taverns as resort;
vsm1.1:45.6: he does not dwell associated with kings … sectarians' disciples, in unbecoming association with laymen;
vsm1.1:45.7:
he cultivates, frequents, honours, such families as are faithful and trusting, who are a solace,
where the yellow cloth glows, where the breeze of sages blows, who wish good, wish well, wish joy,
wish surcease of bondage, for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, for male and female devotees—this is called proper resort.
vsm1.1:45.8:
Thus he is furnished with, fully furnished with, provided with, fully provided with, supplied
with, possessed of, endowed with, this proper conduct and this proper resort.
vsm1.1:45.9: Hence it is said, ’Possessed of the proper conduct and resort’” (Vibh 246–47).
vsm1.1:46.1: 46. Furthermore, proper conduct and resort should also be understood here in the following way;
vsm1.1:46.2: for improper conduct is twofold as bodily and verbal.
vsm1.1:46.3: Herein, what is bodily improper conduct?
vsm1.1:46.4:
“Here someone acts disrespectfully before the Community, and he stands jostling elder bhikkhus, sits jostling them, stands in front
of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, talks standing up, talks waving his arms …
vsm1.1:46.5:
walks with sandals while elder bhikkhus walk without sandals, walks on a high walk while they
walk on a low walk, walks on a walk while they walk on the ground …
vsm1.1:46.6: stands pushing elder bhikkhus, sits pushing them, prevents new bhikkhus from getting a seat …
vsm1.1:46.7: and in the bath house … without asking elder bhikkhus he puts wood on the stove … bolts the door …
vsm1.1:46.8:
and at the bathing place he enters the water jostling elder bhikkhus, enters it in front of them,
bathes jostling them, bathes in front of them, comes out jostling them, comes out in front of them …
vsm1.1:46.9: and entering inside a house he goes jostling elder bhikkhus, goes in front of them, pushing forward he goes in front of them …
vsm1.1:46.10:
and where families have inner private screened rooms in which the women of the family … the girls of the family, sit,
there he enters abruptly, and he strokes a child's head” (Nidd I 228–29). This is called bodily improper conduct.
vsm1.1:47.1: 47. Herein, what is verbal improper conduct?
vsm1.1:47.2:
“Here someone acts disrespectfully before the Community. Without asking elder bhikkhus he talks on the Dhamma,
answers questions, recites the Pātimokkha, talks standing up, talks waving his arms …
vsm1.1:47.3: having entered inside a house, he speaks to a woman or a girl thus: ‘You, so-and-so of such-and-such a clan, what is there?
vsm1.1:47.4:
Is there rice gruel? Is there cooked rice? Is there any hard food to eat? What shall we drink?
What hard food shall we eat? What soft food shall we eat?
vsm1.1:47.5: Or what will you give me?’—he chatters like this” (Nidd I 230). This is called verbal improper conduct.
vsm1.1:48.1: 48. Proper conduct should be understood in the opposite sense to that.
vsm1.1:48.2:
Furthermore, a bhikkhu is respectful, deferential, possessed of conscience and shame,
wears his inner robe properly, wears his upper robe properly,
vsm1.1:48.3:
his manner inspires confidence whether in moving forwards or backwards, looking ahead or aside,
bending or stretching, his eyes are downcast, he has (a good) deportment,
vsm1.1:48.4:
he guards the doors of his sense faculties, knows the right measure in eating, is devoted to wakefulness,
possesses mindfulness and full awareness, wants little, is contented, is strenuous, is a careful observer of good
behaviour, and treats the teachers with great respect. This is called (proper) conduct.
vsm1.1:48.5: This firstly is how (proper) conduct should be understood.
vsm1.1:49.1: 49. (Proper) resort is of three kinds: (proper) resort as support, (proper) resort as guarding, and (proper) resort as anchoring.
vsm1.1:49.2: Herein, what is (proper) resort as support? A good friend who exhibits the instances of talk,
vsm1.1:49.3:
in whose presence one hears what has not been heard, corrects what has been heard,
gets rid of doubt, rectifies one's view, and gains confidence;
vsm1.1:49.4: or by training under whom one grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity and understanding—
vsm1.1:49.5: this is called (proper) resort as support.
vsm1.1:50.1:
50. What is (proper) resort as guarding? Here “A bhikkhu, having entered inside a house, having
gone into a street, goes with downcast eyes, seeing the length of a plough yoke, restrained,
vsm1.1:50.2: not looking at an elephant, not looking at a horse, a carriage, a pedestrian, a woman, a man,
vsm1.1:50.3: not looking up, not looking down, not staring this way and that” (Nidd I 474). This is called (proper) resort as guarding.
vsm1.1:51.1: 51. What is (proper) resort as anchoring? It is the four foundations of mindfulness on which the mind is anchored;
vsm1.1:51.2:
for this is said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, what is a bhikkhu's resort, his own native place?
It is these four foundations of mindfulness” (S V 148).
vsm1.1:51.3: This is called (proper) resort as anchoring.
vsm1.1:51.4: Being thus furnished with … endowed with, this (proper) conduct and this (proper) resort,
vsm1.1:51.5: he is also on that account called “one possessed of (proper) conduct and resort.”
vsm1.1:52.1: 52. Seeing fear in the slightest fault (§42):
vsm1.1:52.2:
one who has the habit (sīla) of seeing fear in faults of the minutest measure, of such kinds as unintentional
contravening of a minor training rule of the Pātimokkha, or the arising of unprofitable thoughts.
vsm1.1:52.3: He trains himself by undertaking (samādāya) the precepts of training:
vsm1.1:52.4: whatever there is among the precepts of training to be trained in, in all that he trains by taking it up rightly (sammā ādāya).
vsm1.1:52.5: And here, as far as the words, “one restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint,”
vsm1.1:52.6: virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is shown by discourse in terms of persons.
vsm1.1:52.7: But all that beginning with the words, “possessed of proper conduct and resort”
vsm1.1:52.8: should be understood as said in order to show the way of practice that perfects that virtue in him who so practices it.
vsm1.1:53.1:
53. (b) Now, as regards the virtue of restraint of faculties shown next to that in the way
beginning, “on seeing a visible object with the eye,”
vsm1.1:53.2: herein he is a bhikkhu established in the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint.
vsm1.1:53.3: On seeing a visible object with the eye:
vsm1.1:53.4:
on seeing a visible object with the eye-consciousness that is capable of seeing visible
objects and has borrowed the name “eye” from its instrument.
vsm1.1:53.5:
But the Ancients (porāṇā) said: “The eye does not see a visible object because it has no mind.
The mind does not see because it has no eyes.
vsm1.1:53.6:
But when there is the impingement of door and object he sees by means of the consciousness that has eye-sensitivity as its physical
basis. Now, (an idiom) such as this is called an ‘accessory locution’ (sasambhārakathā), like ‘He shot him with his bow,’ and so on.
vsm1.1:53.7: So the meaning here is this: ‘On seeing a visible object with eye-consciousness.’”
vsm1.1:54.1:
54. Apprehends neither the signs: he does not apprehend the sign of woman or man, or any
sign that is a basis for defilement such as the sign of beauty, etc.;
vsm1.1:54.2: he stops at what is merely seen.
vsm1.1:54.4:
he does not apprehend any aspect classed as hand, foot, smile, laughter, talk, looking ahead,
looking aside, etc., which has acquired the name “particular” (anubyañjana) because of its particularizing
(anu anu byañjanato) defilements, because of its making them manifest themselves.
vsm1.1:54.5: He only apprehends what is really there.
vsm1.1:54.6: Like the Elder Mahā Tissa who dwelt at Cetiyapabbata.
vsm1.1:55.1: 55. It seems that as the elder was on his way from Cetiyapabbata to Anurādhapura for alms,
vsm1.1:55.2:
a certain daughter-in-law of a clan, who had quarrelled with her husband and had set out
early from Anurādhapura all dressed up and tricked out like a celestial nymph to go to her relatives’ home,
saw him on the road, and being low-minded, she laughed a loud laugh.
vsm1.1:55.3: Wondering “What is that?” the elder looked up and
vsm1.1:55.4: finding in the bones of her teeth the perception of foulness (ugliness), he reached Arahantship.
vsm1.1:55.5:
Hence it was said: “He saw the bones that were her teeth, And kept in mind his first
perception; And standing on that very spot The elder became an Arahant.”
vsm1.1:55.6: But her husband, who was going after her, saw the elder and asked, “Venerable sir, did you by any chance see a woman?”
vsm1.1:55.7:
The elder told him: “Whether it was a man or woman That went by I noticed not, But only
that on this high road There goes a group of bones.”
vsm1.1:56.1: 56. As to the words through which, etc., the meaning is:
vsm1.1:56.2:
by reason of which, because of which non-restraint of the eye faculty, if he, if that person, left the eye
faculty unguarded, remained with the eye door unclosed by the door-panel of mindfulness,
vsm1.1:56.3: these states of covetousness, etc., might invade, might pursue, might threaten, him.
vsm1.1:56.4: He enters upon the way of its restraint: he enters upon the way of closing that eye faculty by the door-panel of mindfulness.
vsm1.1:56.5: It is the same one of whom it is said he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.
vsm1.1:57.1: 57. Herein, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the actual eye faculty,
vsm1.1:57.2: since neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness arises in dependence on eye-sensitivity.
vsm1.1:57.3: On the contrary when a visible datum as object comes into the eye’s focus,
vsm1.1:57.4:
then, after the life-continuum has arisen twice and ceased, the functional mind-element
accomplishing the function of adverting arises and ceases.
vsm1.1:57.5: After that, eye-consciousness with the function of seeing; after that, resultant mind-element with the function of receiving;
vsm1.1:57.6:
after that, resultant root-causeless mind-consciousness-element with the function of investigating; after that, functional
root-causeless mind-consciousness-element accomplishing the function of determining arises and ceases.
vsm1.1:57.8: Herein, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint on the occasion of the life-continuum,
vsm1.1:57.9: or on any of the occasions beginning with adverting.
vsm1.1:57.10:
But there is non-restraint if unvirtuousness or forgetfulness or unknowing or impatience or idleness
arises at the moment of impulsion.
vsm1.1:57.11: When this happens, it is called “non-restraint in the eye faculty.”
vsm1.1:58.2: Because when this happens, the door is not guarded, nor are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series.
vsm1.1:58.4: Just as, when a city’s four gates are not secured, although inside the city house doors, storehouses, rooms, etc., are secured,
vsm1.1:58.5: yet all property inside the city is unguarded and unprotected
vsm1.1:58.6: since robbers coming in by the city gates can do as they please,
vsm1.1:58.7:
so too, when unvirtuousness, etc., arise in impulsion in which there is no restraint, then the door too is unguarded, and so
also are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.
vsm1.1:58.8: But when virtue, etc., has arisen in it, then the door too is guarded
vsm1.1:58.9: and so also are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.
vsm1.1:58.11: Just as, when the city gates are secured, although inside the city the houses, etc., are not secured,
vsm1.1:58.12: yet all property inside the city is well guarded, well protected,
vsm1.1:58.13: since when the city gates are shut there is no ingress for robbers,
vsm1.1:58.14:
so too, when virtue, etc., have arisen in impulsion, the door too is guarded and so also
are the life-continuum and the consciousnesses of the cognitive series beginning with adverting.
vsm1.1:58.15: Thus although it actually arises at the moment of impulsion, it is nevertheless called “restraint in the eye faculty.”
vsm1.1:59.1: 59. So also as regards the phrases on hearing a sound with the ear and so on.
vsm1.1:59.2:
So it is this virtue, which in brief has the characteristic of avoiding apprehension of signs entailing
defilement with respect to visible objects, etc., that should be understood as virtue of restraint of faculties.
